Where it began

Allan Border was born on 27 July 1955 in Cremorne, on Sydney's North Shore, and grew up close by in Mosman with three brothers. The family home faced Mosman Oval, so a game was never far away, and he usually played in teams two or three years older than he was.

Baseball helped too. It sharpened his fielding and his cross-bat shots. At sixteen he made his grade debut for Mosman as a left-arm spinner batting at number nine, a long way from where he finished. He first played for New South Wales in January 1977.

The player

His Test debut came at Melbourne in the 1978–79 Ashes, and he needed more than half an hour to make three runs, a fair preview of a patient career. After missing one early Test he played the next 153 in a row. In all he played 156 Tests between 1978 and 1994 and scored 11,174 runs at 50.56, with 27 hundreds, 63 fifties and a best of 205. When he retired, no batsman had made more Test runs. He also held 155 catches.

In Lahore he made 150 not out and 153 in the same Test, the first batsman to pass 150 in both innings. He took over the captaincy in 1984–85, with the side at a low ebb, and went on to lead Australia in 93 Tests: 32 won, 22 lost and 39 drawn. Under him Australia won the 1987 World Cup and, in 1989, the Ashes in England 4–0.

What made him special

Nobody bought a ticket for the elegance. Border crouched, waited and punished anything short, and he is remembered for grit rather than grace. Yet he could attack, he used quick feet against spin, and he was a fine slip catcher. Above all he could hold out for hours while others failed around him.

His bowling is the friendly joke. As captain he seldom gave himself a turn, and after 99 Tests he had 16 wickets. Then, in the match that made him the first Australian to play 100 Tests, he took 7 for 46 and 4 for 50 against West Indies at Sydney, and Australia won. Perhaps he should have asked himself sooner.

Away from the middle

In 1994–95 he helped Queensland win the Sheffield Shield for the first time, and he later served as an Australian selector. His name is all over the game: Australia's cricketer of the year receives the Allan Border Medal, Tests between India and Australia are played for the Border–Gavaskar Trophy, and a bronze statue of him was unveiled at the Gabba in December 2021. He was Australian of the Year in 1989 and was among the first players inducted into the ICC Cricket Hall of Fame. To team-mates he was simply A.B.

And finally

As a boy he lived just across the street from Mosman Oval. Years later it was renamed the Allan Border Oval, which makes it one of the shortest journeys in cricket from the backyard to the honours board.
